name: Gareth Jensen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so feel free to tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you tell me a bit about yourself?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm Gareth, 27, and I'm the junior marketer at Tidewell, a small brand that makes canned sparkling teas, about twenty staff in total. I live with my boyfriend Sanjay, who's a software tester, in a rented two-bed near the canal. I've been at Tidewell eight months, after a year of temping in a call centre.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Walk me through a normal working day. What do you do, what do you like, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My day is mostly paid social: I plan the ads, write five or six versions of every caption, and test which one gets people to click. I use AI tools all day, for first drafts, for resizing images, for summarising what people say in comments. I'll be honest, my writing on its own isn't great yet, and the AI tools cover for that a lot. What wears me out is our founder, Ruth, changing the brand voice every second week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, fair enough, it's a good assistant, not a genius. I'd probably post a thread about the tools I still find useful, because people ask me. At work I'd tell Ruth we can stop panicking and get back to the summer launch.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be fine, maybe even better off. I'm the one who knows the tools, and if they plateau, that knowledge stays useful for years. My real pressure is that Tidewell is small and still not making a profit, so the job depends on the next funding round.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing what I'm doing and get properly good at the writing itself, without leaning on the tools. I'd ask Ruth if I can sit in on the funding pitch prep, to understand the money side. And I'd keep my four months of savings where they are.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pretty relaxed. I'd still glance at the company bank balance in my head now and then, but that's startup life. Honestly I'd find it a bit boring.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the tools cover for your writing. If they plateau, does that become a problem?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit, yes. The tools plateauing means everyone else catches up on using them, and then the difference is who writes better. That's my weak spot, so I'd take an evening copywriting class at the college on Mill Street.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does Sanjay feel about all this?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sanjay's more nervous than me, because software testing is very routine. In a plateau world he'd relax too. We'd probably finally book the trip to his grandparents we keep putting off.

I'd post a thread on the **tools** I still find useful.
think: His **tool skills** stay useful for years in a plateau.

Ask to sit in on the **funding pitch** preparation.
feel: Keeps half an eye on the **company bank balance**.

Book the delayed trip to Sanjay's grandparents

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the moment to make sure workers share the gains. If a tool makes a team twice as fast, people should get shorter weeks, not pink slips. I'd post that, and I'd say it to Ruth too, carefully.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think I'm probably okay, because I'm the person who already runs the tools. At a small brand like Tidewell, they'll want one person who can do the work of three with software, and that's me. The risk is that a bigger brand's AI agency undercuts all of us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd write up a plan for Ruth showing how I could run all our channels with the tools, before she thinks of it herself. I'd spend about 300 on a proper course in AI ad tools and analytics. And I'd start freelancing for two local cafés on weekends, so I'm not dependent on one startup.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Quietly confident, with a small guilty feeling. If I'm the one who does the work of three, two other people somewhere didn't get hired. I don't love that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You talked about workers sharing the gains, but you'd also pitch yourself as doing three people's work. How do those fit?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: They don't fit neatly, you're right. I think the system should share the gains, but until it does, I've got rent and I'm not going to be the one left out. I'd vote for the shorter week and still pitch the do-three-jobs plan on Monday.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who outside work would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My sister Kat, who's a receptionist at a dental clinic, because booking and answering calls is exactly what the card says. I'd sit with her and show her the tools. She'd hate it, but she'd let me.

S1.quote: I'd vote for the shorter week and still pitch the do-three-jobs plan on Monday.
fieldNote: He openly admits the gap between his **politics** and his **pitch**.

steps.text: Pitch the founder a plan to run all channels with AI tools

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need emergency rules: a pause on mass layoffs, a tax on AI profits, and income support straight away. I'd go to marches and post constantly. At work I'd say I'll help Tidewell adapt but not to cut people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, being good with the AI tools stops mattering when the tools don't need me. If AI can do any thinking work, it can run Tidewell's ads without a junior in the middle. I'd give my job maybe a year after 2028.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first month I'd talk to Sanjay about both our jobs, because we're both screen workers. I'd stop freelancing for cafés and offer to set up AI systems for small businesses instead, while that's still a thing people pay for. I'd also look at hands-on work, maybe brewing at Tidewell's canning partner, since robots are three years behind.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Like being good at a game right before they change the rules. I'm adaptive, but two years is fast even for me. And we'd have two incomes at risk in one house.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said brewing at the canning partner. Have you ever done hands-on work like that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only at a summer job packing boxes at a warehouse when I was nineteen. I liked being tired in my body instead of my head. I'd ask Ruth to introduce me to the guy who runs the canning line.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you and Sanjay cut first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The second bedroom, which is my office. We'd move to a one-bed and save about 250 a month. Then the car, if one of us lost work.

I'd help Tidewell adapt but **not cut people**.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is short but it's enough to build a safety net if governments start now. I'd join a union, which I've never done, and push for retraining funds. Online I'd share practical guides, not just fear.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd probably have a good three years where my tool skills are valuable, then it drops off. I'd use those years to save hard and build something that isn't just me at a laptop. I'm curious more than scared, but I'm not naive.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd try to move from marketing into something like community or events at a bigger brand, where you need a face. I'd aim to save six months of expenses by 2029. Sanjay and I would talk about whether one of us retrains into a hands-on trade, maybe him as an electrician.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but with energy. Five years feels like a sprint I can actually run. I'd be tired but not lost.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said one of you might become an electrician. Why him and not you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because Sanjay's good with his hands and hates screens anyway, and I'm better with people. If one of us has hands-on work, that's three extra years of safe income for the house. I'd stay in people-facing marketing while he trains.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does six months of savings mean for you in money?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: About 9,000, so roughly double what we've got now. That means no holidays and no new phones for a couple of years. Fine by me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the best of the AGI versions, and we should use the decade to rebuild how work and income are shared. I'd talk about a four-day week, retraining accounts, things like that. At work I'd volunteer to train people on the tools.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I'd climb a bit in marketing for five or six years, then switch. By 2036 I'd be 37, and I want a skill that isn't on a screen by then. Ten years is long enough to train properly, even part-time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay at Tidewell or a bigger brand, keep using the tools every day, and get good at the strategy side. Around year three I'd start a part-time course, maybe in physiotherapy, which is hands-on and people-facing. And we'd keep saving toward a deposit, but somewhere cheap.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calmer, though the end point is the same. It's a long runway. I'd still feel the clock now and then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Physiotherapy is a big jump from canned tea ads. Where does that come from?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My mum had a bad back for years and the physio was the only person who actually helped. Physiotherapy is a job where you need hands and you need to read people. Robots might do it in 2039, but by then I'd have ten good years in it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would kids change any of this?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We've talked about adopting in our thirties. A decade of warning would let us plan that around my training, rather than in the middle of a crisis. That matters to me more than the job.

I'd volunteer to **train colleagues** on the tools.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because Sanjay and I both work on screens and two years isn't enough for either of us to switch. What would help is income support while people retrain, and a rule that companies can't cut everyone at once.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe how being good at the tools feels safe until it doesn't. I'm the AI guy at work, and people assume I'm fine. Being the AI guy at work only helps until the AI doesn't need a guy.

headlineQuote: Being the AI guy at work only helps until the AI doesn't need a guy.
portrait: Gareth is a **27-year-old junior** at a small canned-tea startup, living with Sanjay, a software tester.
He uses **AI daily** and admits it covers for his weak writing.
In slow change he sees himself as the **tool person** a small brand keeps.
Fast AGI scares him because **both incomes** in the house are screen work.
With time he'd move toward **physiotherapy** and plan adoption with Sanjay.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because both he and Sanjay work on **screens**.
whatWouldHelp: A rule stopping companies from **cutting everyone** at once.
